title: General Overview
subject: Lymphoid System
introMarkdown:
The lymphoid system performs three jobs that initially seem unrelated: it recovers excess fluid from tissues, helps defend the body against infection, and carries much of the fat absorbed by the small intestine back toward the bloodstream. Together, its vessels, lymph nodes, lymphoid organs, and immune cells create a transport and surveillance network that reaches nearly every region of the body.

The **lymphatic system** refers especially to the vessels and fluid-transport network; **lymphoid tissues and organs** house and support immune cells. Immunity also involves blood, bone marrow, epithelial barriers, and cells outside lymphatic vessels. Chapter 22 studies these interconnected processes together.

sections.title: Three Jobs, One System
sections.markdown:
The three major functions are:

- **Fluid recovery:** Return excess fluid and escaped proteins from the spaces between cells to the bloodstream, limiting tissue swelling (*edema*).
- **Immune defense:** Transport material from tissues to lymph nodes, where immune cells can detect threats and coordinate responses. Lymphoid tissues also produce, mature, and maintain lymphocytes.
- **Fat transport:** Carry much of the absorbed long-chain dietary fat from intestinal *lacteals* through lymphatic vessels into venous blood.

The same network can recover fluid from your ankle, deliver a potential pathogen to a nearby lymph node, and transport absorbed fat from your intestines. These functions overlap rather than operating as three separate systems.

sections.title: From Blood Plasma to Interstitial Fluid to Lymph
sections.markdown:
Blood capillaries exchange fluid with the surrounding tissues. When fluid leaves the capillary and enters the space between cells, it is called **interstitial fluid**. When some of that fluid enters a lymphatic capillary, it becomes **lymph**. The names describe **where the fluid is**, not three completely different substances.

Unlike blood capillaries, initial lymphatic capillaries start as blind-ended vessels. Their overlapping endothelial cells can open inward when the surrounding tissue pressure rises, allowing fluid and some larger material to enter. The lymphatic network eventually returns that fluid to blood.

**Basic route:** Blood plasma → interstitial fluid → lymphatic capillaries → larger lymphatic vessels → lymphatic ducts → veins.

sections.title: The One-Way Route Back to Blood
sections.markdown:
Once fluid becomes lymph, it moves through collecting vessels equipped with **one-way valves**. There is no single lymphatic heart. Skeletal-muscle movements, breathing-related pressure changes, nearby arterial pulsations, and contractions of lymphatic vessel walls help propel the fluid while valves discourage backflow.

Most lymph returns through the **thoracic duct**, which drains the lower body and the upper-left portion of the body. The **right lymphatic duct** drains the upper-right region. Both ultimately empty near the junctions of the internal jugular and subclavian veins on their respective sides.

The **cisterna chyli** is an expanded collecting region commonly found near the beginning of the thoracic duct. It receives lymph from the lower body and intestinal region.

sections.title: Three Major Lymphocyte Classes
sections.markdown:
**Lymphocytes** are immune cells that recognize, coordinate responses to, or destroy threats. Chapter 22 emphasizes three major classes:

- **B cells:** Participate in *humoral* or antibody-mediated immunity. When appropriately activated, some become **plasma cells**, which secrete antibodies; others contribute to immune memory.
- **T cells:** Participate in *cell-mediated* immunity. **Helper T cells** coordinate responses, while **cytotoxic T cells** can kill infected or abnormal cells. Other T-cell populations help regulate responses.
- **Natural killer (NK) cells:** Provide rapid **innate**, relatively nonspecific surveillance for certain infected, stressed, or abnormal cells without requiring the same prior antigen-specific activation as a T cell.

All three arise from blood-forming stem cells. B cells develop primarily in **bone marrow**, while T-cell precursors mature in the **thymus**.

sections.title: Where Immune Cells Develop and Meet
sections.markdown:
The lecture's three principal **encapsulated lymphoid organs** are the **lymph nodes, thymus, and spleen**. These have different responsibilities:

- **Lymph nodes** filter **lymph** and help initiate immune responses to material arriving from tissues.
- **Thymus** provides the specialized environment where developing **T cells** mature.
- **Spleen** monitors **blood**, supports immune responses to blood-borne antigens, and removes aged or abnormal red blood cells.

The body also contains less distinctly encapsulated lymphoid tissues, including **tonsils**, **Peyer's patches**, the **appendix**, and other **mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)**. These sample and respond to material encountered near mucosal surfaces. Bone marrow is also an essential primary lymphoid organ in broader immunology terminology.

sections.title: The Immediate Defenses
sections.markdown:
Not every threat requires a highly specific antibody response. The body begins with **nonspecific (innate) defenses** that act quickly and provide the conditions for later targeted responses.

The instructor groups them into **seven categories**: physical barriers, phagocytic cells, immunological surveillance, interferons, complement, inflammation, and fever.

For example, damaged skin can trigger **inflammation**. Local blood vessels dilate and become more permeable; chemical signals recruit phagocytes; and the affected area may become red, warm, swollen, and painful. **Natural killer cells** can detect certain abnormal cells, while **complement proteins** can tag microbes for removal or help damage their membranes.

sections.title: Specific Recognition and Immune Memory
sections.markdown:
**Adaptive immunity** is more selective. B and T lymphocytes recognize particular molecular targets called **antigens** or antigen-derived fragments. **Antigen-presenting cells** help activate appropriate T cells, which can coordinate other immune cells. Activated B cells can produce antibodies that bind specific targets and assist their removal.

A first exposure generally takes time to build a strong adaptive response. Some activated cells persist as **memory cells**, allowing a faster or stronger response if the same antigen is encountered again. This is the central principle behind immune memory and many vaccines.

The immune system must also maintain **tolerance** to normal tissues. A strong response against the wrong target can be harmful, which is why the immune system needs mechanisms that both activate and restrain its cells.

sections.title: What You Should Be Able to Identify
sections.markdown:
For anatomy and model identification, prioritize the **thoracic duct**, **right lymphatic duct**, **cisterna chyli**, **cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph-node groups**, **thymus**, **spleen**, and **tonsils**. For tissue diagrams, distinguish the **lymph-node capsule, cortex, paracortex, medulla, afferent vessels, efferent vessel, and hilum**; the **red and white pulp of the spleen**; and the **cortex and medulla of the thymus**.

For physiology, be able to explain the route lymph takes back into the blood, distinguish **B cells, T cells, and NK cells**, and contrast **innate versus adaptive immunity** and **primary versus secondary immune responses**.

The **Deep Dive** develops these structures and mechanisms in detail. **Exam Cram** will organize the same Chapter 22 material around the instructor's study-guide questions.
